cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Food poisoning is illness caused by eating food contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, or toxins.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: The main food poisoning bacteria include: Salmonella, E. coli (especially O157), Campylobacter, Staphylococcus aureus, and Clostridium perfringens.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Salmonella is commonly found in raw poultry and eggs; symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal cramps.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: E. coli O157 is found in undercooked minced beef and unpasteurised milk; it can cause severe kidney damage (haemolytic uraemic syndrome).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Campylobacter is the most common cause of bacterial food poisoning in the UK, often from undercooked poultry.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Staphylococcus aureus produces toxins in food; it is carried on skin and in nasal passages and transfers to food through poor hand hygiene.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Clostridium perfringens forms heat-resistant spores; it thrives in food left at room temperature (e.g. large batches of cooked meat).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Norovirus is a virus (not a bacterium) causing 'winter vomiting bug'; it spreads through contaminated food and poor hygiene.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Food poisoning can be caused by infection (eating live bacteria) or intoxication (eating pre-formed toxins in food).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness
cards.back: Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria from one food (usually raw) to another, and is the most common cause of food poisoning.

cards.front: What should you know about food preparation & nutrition exam tips — food poisoning & food-borne illness?
cards.back: 1. For Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness questions, show every step of your working clearly — method marks count even if the final answer is wrong 2. Check your answer makes sense in context (estimation, units, reasonableness) 3. Use correct mathematical notation and state formulae before substituting values 4. If a Food Poisoning & Food-Borne Illness question asks you to 'prove' or 'show', write a logical chain of reasoning with a conclusion line 5. For problem-solving, identify the topic first, then recall the relevant method
